solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Here's our phone number — is that corny?

definitions.note: a phrase, read as two words of instruction
definitions.meaning: first reading: what a firm prints beside its number, telling you to ring them

definitions.note: adjective in the clue, noun answer
definitions.meaning: second reading: a hardened patch of skin on the foot, akin to a corn

explanation.surface: Someone sees a company's cheesy 'here's our number' line and asks whether it's a bit naff.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as CALL US it is the line under a phone number; run together it is a patch of hard skin. 'Corny' looks like 'trite' but points to corns on the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A corn is a small, hard thickening of skin, a type of the broader thickened-skin patch named by the answer.

clue.text: Hoover, say, has got stuck in like US president

indicators.note: a thing stuck in something else sits wedged inside it

parts.note: 'as' means 'like', in the sense of resembling
the Hoover Dam is an example of a dam

explanation.surface: A vacuum cleaner jammed into something, oddly compared to an American president.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoover suggests the vacuum cleaner or J. Edgar or Herbert Hoover the president; here it is the dam on the Colorado River.
explanation.definitionFit: John Adams and John Quincy Adams were the second and sixth holders of the American presidency.

clue.text: So fired without hesitation?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in the manner of something fired from a gun
second meaning: very quickly and eagerly

explanation.walkthrough: 'So fired' reads like sacking someone on the spot; it is the literal sense of the phrase, the manner of a bullet leaving a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at once and willingly, as in agreeing to an offer immediately, with no pause for thought.

clue.text: Drink: Warhol should can it!

parts.note: 'can it!' means 'be quiet!', which is 'sh!'
Andy Warhol, the pop artist

explanation.surface: Someone tells Andy Warhol to put a drink in a can, or to shut up about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Telling Andy Warhol to can it is 'Sh, Andy'. Warhol's soup cans make 'can' look literal. A shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, a British pub drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Shandy is a beverage of beer topped up with lemonade or ginger beer, popular in British pubs.

clue.text: Venture by enchanting company in English city

parts.note: a coven is a gathering of witches, who cast spells
to venture is to try or attempt

explanation.surface: A business venture by a charming firm based in some English city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enchanting company' reads as a delightful firm; enchanting here means casting spells, so the company is witches.
explanation.definitionFit: Coventry is a large cathedral city in the West Midlands of England, known for its car industry.

clue.text: Whatever racehorse I'm on in horsing around!

indicators.note: horsing around is fooling about, so the letters are played with and jumbled

parts.note: the fifteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A jockey declares they don't care which mount they get, all while larking about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whatever' at the front looks like part of the jockey's speech; it is the definition, meaning regardless of circumstances.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means regardless of conditions or whatever happens, from the idea of going ahead in any weather.

clue.text: Front I dispensed with, gone

parts.note: the van is the front, as in vanguard
taken as written
to shed something is to get rid of it

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned a front or pretence, and now it has disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: VAN for the front comes from vanguard, the leading part of an army.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has disappeared from sight or existence is described with either word, both past participles.

clue.text: I say I don't want them near me, dark clouds

indicators.note: what I say is heard, so the spoken form counts, not the spelling

parts.words: I don't want them near me
parts.note: NIMBY stands for 'not in my back yard', the protest against nearby development

explanation.surface: A grumpy resident objects to something looming nearby, likened to gathering storm clouds.
explanation.walkthrough: A NIMBY is someone who objects to development near their own home.
explanation.definitionFit: Nimbi is the plural of nimbus, the term for a dark grey rain-bearing cloud layer.

clue.text: Crude, when by inference?

parts.note: surface reading: an adjective for something roughly made
setter's reading: the answer, read as an instruction, says a jumbled version of the letters of 'when' gives the second word

explanation.surface: Someone asks how they're meant to deduce a vague time.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the second word is an anagram of WHEN, and the first word is an anagram signal, so the answer describes how to get WHEN from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something roughly shaped by axe or chisel and left unfinished is crude in form, unpolished and unrefined.

clue.text: Help cheat in game

parts.note: to back someone is to support them
to gammon is an old word for to hoax or deceive

explanation.surface: Someone assisting a player to cheat during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: GAMMON as a verb for to humbug is old British slang; it is also a winning margin in this board game.
explanation.definitionFit: Backgammon is an ancient board game for two players moving counters by dice throws.

clue.text: Attack in African country briefly stopped by leader in uprising

indicators.note: made brief, the word is cut short by its final letter
a gap that is stopped is plugged, with something filling the middle

parts.note: Mali, in West Africa, without its last letter

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A violent assault in an African nation was swiftly halted by the head of a rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' looks like it modifies 'stopped', a short-lived attack, but it trims Mali.
explanation.definitionFit: To savage or batter someone fiercely, as a bear or a lion does, is a form of violent physical assault.

clue.text: Cuban for example who has been vilified by me

parts.note: the speaker refers to themself
to vilify is to slander, read here as the present-tense verb

explanation.surface: Someone from Cuba whom the speaker has repeatedly badmouthed.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a whole thought: if I SLANDER you, you have been vilified by me. Read as one word, it is someone from an island.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuba is a Caribbean island nation, so any Cuban is an inhabitant of an island, an example of the category.

clue.text: Small and delicate — so?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
light means delicate, as in a light touch

explanation.surface: Someone describes a dainty little thing and shrugs, asking what of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The '— so?' says the pieces S and LIGHT, put together, also describe the answer, which is small and delicate itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A slight figure is slender and frail-looking, so the adjective covers both little size and fragile build.

clue.text: Touch zip

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a small amount, as a touch of salt
second meaning: energy and verve, or a fast run

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like verbs, touching and fastening a zip; both are nouns here.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny added quantity of an ingredient and lively spirit or a sudden sprint are both senses of the word.

clue.text: A military alliance secure when set up in part of 28 across, say?

parts.note: taken as written
the North Atlantic Treaty Organization

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: to nail something is to fix it firmly

explanation.surface: A defence pact shores up its position in a region of a neighbouring country.
explanation.walkthrough: 28 across is TURKEY; Anatolia is its large Asian part. The 'say' allows that someone from there is one example of the description.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatolia is the peninsula forming most of modern Turkey, so a resident or thing from there is located within that region.

clue.text: Something frozen, cheese melting in it

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: taken as written, split around the jumble

indicators.note: melting changes form and runs, so the letters lose their shape and reform

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: Some frozen food with cheese melting inside it, like a ready meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Melting' sits awkwardly beside 'frozen', which makes the surface read as cooking rather than an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A vast layer of glacial ice covering land, as in Greenland or Antarctica, is a large frozen expanse.

clue.text: Stand up, as might pitcher?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: of an argument, to survive scrutiny
second meaning: what a jug does with its liquid contents

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitcher' suggests the baseball player; it is a jug. 'Stand up' is about an argument surviving examination, not rising to your feet.
explanation.definitionFit: An argument that bears scrutiny is said to be sound, and a jug's job is literally containing liquid without leaking.

clue.text: Introduce American hero?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to fit something in between two others
second meaning: in the US a hero is a long filled roll

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hero' looks like a brave American; in American English it is a long submarine roll with fillings.
explanation.definitionFit: To squeeze an item between two others is to insert it, and a hero sub is a type of filled bread roll.

clue.text: Capital adversary invested in cereal

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: sago is a starchy grain-like food from palm pith
an anti is someone opposed to something

explanation.surface: An opponent puts money into a breakfast-cereal firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money, fitting 'invested'; it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Santiago is the seat of government of Chile, a capital city in South America.

clue.text: Flooring material in centre of oblong houses

indicators.note: to house something is to hold it within, so one piece encloses another
the centre is the middle, so only the two central letters are kept

parts.note: the middle two of the six letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: The floor covering found in the middle of rectangular homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Houses' reads as a noun, buildings; it is a verb meaning holds. 'In' looks like a link word but is a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Lino is short for linoleum, a hard-wearing sheet floor covering made from linseed oil and cork.

clue.text: Drive away, passing through Faro in truck

indicators.note: something passing through spans parts of several words, so the answer runs across them

parts.note: letters running from the town into the vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone drives off in a lorry, travelling through Faro in Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: Faro is a city in the Algarve. The answer is an archaic Shakespearean word, best known from 'Aroint thee, witch!' in Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: The old imperative means begone, so it is a command used to send someone off or banish them.

clue.text: Lazy old walk into land of sleep

indicators.note: something going into a place ends up inside it

parts.note: the land of Nod is the realm of sleep
O is the standard abbreviation for old
to go is to move, as on foot

explanation.surface: An idle old person strolls off to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The land of Nod is a jokey English phrase for sleep, from nodding off.
explanation.definitionFit: A worthless good-for-nothing person, idle and useless, is described with this hyphenated adjective.

clue.text: Two bovines, the second with head slightly back in lake

indicators.text: the second with head slightly back
indicators.note: the first letter of the latter item moves one step back through the alphabet, replacing it

parts.note: an ox and a cow, both cattle

explanation.surface: A pair of cattle, one tossing its head back while wading in a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slightly back' means one letter earlier in the alphabet: C becomes B, so COW turns into BOW.
explanation.definitionFit: An oxbow is a curved lake left behind when a meandering river cuts off one of its loops, short for oxbow lake.

clue.text: Boater has taken more than one craft backwards, eh?

indicators.note: going backwards means reading from the end to the start

parts.note: crafts are arts, plural
'eh?' asks 'what?'

explanation.surface: A rower has piloted several boats, but reversing them, puzzled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boater' and 'craft' paint a boating scene; craft here is skill, and a boater is a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A boater is a flat-topped stiff hat woven from straw with a ribbon band, once worn for punting.

clue.text: A nozzle evolved

parts.note: taken as written
a rose is the perforated spray head on a watering can or shower

explanation.surface: A spray nozzle that developed over time.
explanation.walkthrough: The rose is the sprinkler head of a watering can, not the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that emerged or came into being gradually can be said to have developed or come about.

clue.text: Fin, say, scales stripped off

indicators.note: stripping removes the outside layer, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: to scale a wall is to climb it

explanation.surface: A fish's fin with its scales removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scales' looks like the fish's skin, matching 'fin'; it is the verb, climbs.
explanation.definitionFit: A fin serves as a fish's appendage for moving, comparable to an arm or leg, hence the 'say' for an example.

clue.text: Launch one past it into country east of India

parts.note: India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: something put into another thing ends up inside it

parts.note: a nation is a country
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Launching someone past it into a country beyond India, as in a send-off.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across answer, east of a piece means after it, so the country follows the India letter; 'one past it' puts I after IT.
explanation.definitionFit: The start or beginning of a project or scheme is its commencement, and both nouns name that first step.

clue.text: Show one off that's attached to heel in blizzards?

definitions.text: Show one off that's attached to heel in blizzards?

indicators.note: something gone off has gone wrong, so the letters are out of order

parts.note: the seven letters to rearrange

indicators.note: the heel is the back end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Showing off an item you strap to your boot heel in heavy snow.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a description: the answer is shown off, attached at the heel, in blizzards. 'Heel' is both the boot part and a last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This broad racket-shaped frame fastened under a boot spreads weight over deep snow, so it is strapped on for walking in storms.

clue.text: Reversal of dreary practice critical for country

indicators.note: a reversal turns the order around, reading from the end

parts.note: a rut is a boring, unvarying routine
key means vital or crucial

explanation.surface: Ending a dull routine is vital for a nation's prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversal of' looks like it governs the whole phrase, but it applies only to the dull routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Turkey is a nation straddling south-eastern Europe and western Asia, with Ankara as its capital.
